summary: Presents example use cases for DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS), which aims to let different DDoS mitigation systems interoperate. The use cases describe how DOTS components interact, how they collaborate and what typical information they exchange. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When a website is flooded with junk traffic, it needs to call for help from defenders. This document gives example stories of who calls whom and what they say, so the call-for-help system can be designed.

subtitle: Example scenarios showing how organizations coordinate to stop DDoS attacks.

tldr.problem: When a DDoS attack occurs, different defense systems (in ISPs, cloud services, enterprises) need to work together quickly, but they use different proprietary systems that cannot easily communicate.
tldr.mechanism: DOTS (DDoS Open Threat Signaling) defines standard ways for these systems to tell each other about attacks and coordinate their defenses. This RFC provides three real-world example scenarios showing how DOTS would be used.
tldr.outcome: By using a common signaling protocol, DDoS defenders can activate mitigation without manual coordination and can share attack information and mitigation status in real time.

today: RFC 8903 is Informational and documents use cases that guided the design of the DOTS protocols. DOTS itself is standardized in RFC 8782 (signal channel) and RFC 8783 (data channel), which provide the actual protocol specifications based on these use cases.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
DDoS attacks flood target systems with traffic, but defending against them is fragmented. ISPs operate independent mitigation systems, enterprises hire third-party protection services, and each system uses different protocols and procedures. When an attack happens, coordination between these defenses is manual, slow, and often incomplete.

This RFC provides five realistic use cases that informed the design of DOTS, a protocol for DDoS mitigation systems to signal each other. The use cases describe how a victim's defense system, an ISP's mitigation system, and third-party defense providers work together. They show what information flows between these actors and in what sequence, which guided the design of the DOTS protocol specifications.
sections.eli5: Different companies try to stop DDoS attacks in different ways, and they need to talk to each other. This document gives example stories of how that conversation might go, so engineers can design a common language.

sections.title: DDoS Mitigation Components
sections.content:
A DDoS Mitigation System (DMS) is hardware or software that detects and stops DDoS attacks. A DDoS Mitigation Service is a subscription offered by an Internet Transit Provider (ITP, typically an ISP) or a third-party service provider. The key actors in DOTS scenarios are:

DOTS Clients run on systems that detect an attack and need help. A client sends a request to start mitigation and later requests to stop it. DOTS Servers run on systems that can help. A server receives mitigation requests, activates defenses, and sends status updates back to the client. A single system might run both client and server code -- for example, an orchestrator that receives attack alerts from sensors and forwards mitigation requests to ISPs or service providers.

The RFC defines a DMS, a DDoS Mitigation Service (the service product), a DDoS Mitigation Service Provider (the company), and an Internet Transit Provider (the ISP delivering traffic). These terms clarify which actors communicate using DOTS.
sections.eli5: A DOTS client says 'I am under attack, help me'. A DOTS server says 'I can help, tell me what is happening.' They talk back and forth using DOTS messages.

sections.title: Upstream ISP Mitigation
sections.content:
In the first major use case, an enterprise network has its own on-premise DDoS defense but contracts with its upstream ISP for additional protection when attacks are very large. The enterprise runs a DOTS client, and the ISP runs a DOTS server.

When traffic to the enterprise exceeds 50% of its ISP link capacity, the enterprise's defense system activates the DOTS client to request mitigation from the ISP. The ISP's DOTS server receives this request and activates its own DMS to filter attack traffic upstream. The ISP's DOTS server periodically sends status updates showing mitigation statistics (how much traffic was blocked, attack patterns detected). When the attack subsides, the enterprise's DOTS client asks the ISP to stop mitigation, and the ISP confirms that mitigation has ended.

The communication between enterprise and ISP might take place on the normal Internet path (in-band), on a dedicated private link (out-of-band), or even over a wireless network. This flexibility lets organizations choose the path that works for their infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Your ISP watches your network. When you say 'too much attack traffic is coming in,' they filter it upstream before it reaches you. You can ask them to stop when the attack ends.

sections.title: Third-Party DDoS Service
sections.content:
The second use case covers enterprises or data centers that contract with a third-party DDoS Mitigation Service Provider (not their ISP). Unlike the upstream ISP, the third-party provider does not naturally sit on the path of the victim's traffic.

When the enterprise is under attack, its DOTS client sends a mitigation request to the third-party provider's DOTS server. The provider and enterprise must have pre-arranged how to redirect traffic to the provider (typically via BGP prefix announcements or DNS redirection). Once traffic reaches the provider, the provider's DMS filters attack traffic and tunnels clean traffic back to the enterprise (often using GRE tunneling).

A key challenge in this use case is that DOTS signaling might itself travel through the ISP carrying the attack traffic, making the signaling path vulnerable. Operators typically arrange for DOTS signaling to use an alternate path that avoids the attacked ISP link.
sections.eli5: A company whose traffic does not normally go through a DDoS defender can arrange to send their traffic through that defender during an attack. The defender and company talk using DOTS to coordinate the diversion and cleanup.

sections.title: DDoS Orchestration
sections.content:
The third use case covers large networks (ISPs, enterprises, data centers) that run an orchestrator to coordinate multiple defense systems. Telemetry and monitoring systems detect attacks and alert the orchestrator using a DOTS client. The orchestrator, running a DOTS server, acknowledges these alerts and analyzes the attack.

When the orchestrator decides to activate mitigation, it sends DOTS client requests to one or more defense systems (its DOTS servers) to activate specific mitigation strategies. Different defense systems might specialize in different attack types. The orchestrator might also send a DOTS request to an upstream ISP or third-party provider. As each defense system reports progress back to the orchestrator, the orchestrator updates a network administrator via a web interface, also using DOTS.

If a DMS reaches its capacity during a severe attack, it can send a DOTS request back to the orchestrator asking for help (offloading). For example, it might ask the orchestrator to configure routers to filter traffic at the edge of the network.
sections.eli5: A big network has a central coordinator that watches for attacks. When sensors see an attack, they tell the coordinator. The coordinator picks the best defense team and tells them to start. If one team gets overwhelmed, they ask the coordinator for help from other teams.
